video_title: John Deere CEO: Autonomous Tractors and Farming's AI Era | Podcast | In Good Company
gist: John May, CEO of John Deere, describes converting a 190-year-old machinery maker into a computer-vision and autonomy company: targeted spraying cuts herbicide use 60%, seed-targeted nitrogen dosing cuts fertilizer cost by two-thirds, and Deere aims for a fully autonomous US corn production system by 2030. He calls 2026 the bottom of the ag cycle — Deere is intentionally underproducing retail demand to clear used inventory — while global trade disruption, not a single-country drought, is what is depressing farm income.

themes.theme: Smart Industrial: selling outcomes, not machines

insights.claim: John Deere's Smart Industrial strategy, launched shortly after John May became CEO in 2019, reoriented the company from building the best individual machine to improving the customer's job outcome, with technology investment aimed explicitly at customer productivity, profitability and sustainability.
insights.speaker: John May, CEO of John Deere
insights.so_what: Frames Deere's capital allocation: R&D and M&A are judged by whether they lower a grower's cost per acre, not by machine unit share — the same outcome-selling pivot investors should test in other industrials.
insights.quote: in the past, what we would do is focus on building the best planter and we wanted to shift to helping our customers plant better than they ever had in the past by leveraging technology

insights.claim: Deere acquired its core AI capability rather than building it, buying Blue River — a computer-vision and advanced-algorithm company working outside agriculture — and repurposing self-driving-car-adjacent technology for plant-level identification and placement instead of vehicle steering.
insights.speaker: John May, CEO of John Deere
insights.so_what: Shows a viable path for industrials to acquire adjacent-industry AI cheaply; the autonomy stack Deere fields is derivative of the AV research base, so AV-sector progress is a read-through for ag autonomy timelines.
insights.quote: if you think about self-driving cars and robo taxis, uh that industry was developing this technology, but we saw a use for it within our industry and really for a totally different outcome

insights.claim: Deere's computer-vision targeted spraying, which distinguishes a weed from a healthy plant and sprays only the weed, reduces herbicide application by 60% versus broadcast spraying the whole field.
insights.speaker: John May, CEO of John Deere
insights.so_what: A 60% cut in herbicide volume across adopted acres is a direct demand headwind for crop-protection chemical volumes even as it raises Deere's technology attach value.
insights.quote: that reduced herbicide application by 60%

insights.claim: By using computer vision to dose nitrogen only where the seed sits rather than free-flowing it into the trench, Deere's planting technology cuts a grower's nitrogen cost by two-thirds.
insights.speaker: John May, CEO of John Deere
insights.so_what: Two-thirds less nitrogen per acre on adopting farms is a structural volume risk for nitrogen fertilizer producers and a quantified ROI story that supports Deere's technology pricing.
insights.quote: that allows our customers to save 2/3 of the nitrogen cost that they would have spent in the past

insights.claim: Deere has replaced hydraulic seed control on planters with independently controlled electric row-unit motors, letting a single machine vary seeding rates row by row — for example 30,000 seeds in one row and 24,000 in the next — based on micro-differences in soil fertility, which May frames as a shift from managing a field to managing every individual plant.
insights.speaker: John May, CEO of John Deere
insights.so_what: The hydraulics-to-electric-actuation shift is the enabling hardware layer for per-plant agronomy: sensor, compute and actuation content then scales with plant count rather than acreage, lifting content per machine.
insights.quote: It's incredible the opportunity to shift from managing a field to managing every individual plant that's out there.

insights.claim: Deere commercially launched its first fully autonomous tillage solution for sale last year and reports strong adoption and results, following driverless tractors in 2022 and a fully autonomous battery-electric machine this year; the pitch is equipment that runs 24 hours a day with no operator in the cab.
insights.speaker: John May, CEO of John Deere
insights.so_what: Autonomy is already revenue-generating at Deere, not a pilot — the adoption curve on tillage is the leading indicator for how fast the rest of the stack monetizes.
insights.quote: last year was the first year we launched an a commercial fully autonomous tillage solution for sale and we've had great adoption and great results as a result of it

insights.claim: Deere's autonomy tech stack is portable across machine types — tractor, combine and sprayer — so each additional production step is an incremental rollout rather than a new development program.
insights.speaker: John May, CEO of John Deere
insights.so_what: Portability implies decreasing marginal cost per autonomous product line and rapid margin leverage once the first stack is amortized.
insights.quote: that tech stack that we developed is portable across a tractor, a combine, a sprayer

insights.claim: Deere's stated ambition is a fully autonomous US corn production system by 2030 — tillage, planting, spraying and harvesting with no operator engaging at all — after which it intends to roll the proven technology across other crops.
insights.speaker: John May, CEO of John Deere
insights.so_what: A dated, crop-specific milestone gives investors a checkable timeline: slippage on corn-by-2030 would push out the entire multi-crop autonomy revenue ramp.
insights.quote: by 2030, we want to have the corn production system, growing corn in the US fully autonomous. That's our goal.

insights.claim: May says the economic driver for farm autonomy is the extreme narrowness of weather-determined planting and harvest windows, which autonomy widens by letting equipment work every available hour rather than by cutting labor cost.
insights.speaker: John May, CEO of John Deere
insights.so_what: Autonomy's value in agriculture is time-window arbitrage rather than labor cost alone, which makes adoption less sensitive to farm wage levels than in trucking or logistics.
insights.quote: the window for farming is so short because of weather

insights.claim: May argues autonomy raises output quality above the individual operator's ceiling and redeploys the farmer's decades of judgment to planning, monitoring multiple machines and field-level optimization — citing his own hay baling, where the bale is only as good as his personal experience.
insights.speaker: John May, CEO of John Deere
insights.so_what: Reframes autonomy as capturing scarce operator judgment rather than displacing labor — the pitch Deere will use to overcome grower resistance and justify subscription pricing.
insights.quote: the end product is going to be as only as good as I am

themes.theme: Pay-per-acre revenue and the right-to-repair reset

insights.claim: Deere is layering pay-by-the-acre and pay-by-the-application SaaS-style models alongside outright purchase specifically to spread expensive technology across more acres, reaching farmers who cannot capitalize the full technology package.
insights.speaker: John May, CEO of John Deere
insights.so_what: The bull case for Deere multiple re-rating rests on recurring revenue mix; watch acre-based subscription disclosure as the metric that would validate it.
insights.quote: by coming up with a pay as you go or a SAS model, it allows us to get this tech on more acres and help more customers

insights.claim: Take rates on Deere's precision technology have doubled versus last year, which May attributes to being able to demonstrate value that hits the farmer's income statement rather than to the pricing model itself.
insights.speaker: John May, CEO of John Deere
insights.so_what: A doubling in take rate during a down farm-income year is evidence that technology attach is counter-cyclical — the single most investable datapoint in the interview.
insights.quote: We're seeing right now uh take rates double from last year on the use of the technology.

insights.claim: Deere's response to the right-to-repair dispute was to ship an AI-backed diagnostic tool that lets customers plug into their own equipment like a dealer technician, identify the failure, and see which parts are needed — leaving the choice of self-repair, a Deere dealer, or an external dealer to the customer.
insights.speaker: John May, CEO of John Deere
insights.so_what: Opening diagnostics concedes some dealer parts-and-service revenue capture; whether Deere's aftermarket margin holds is the test of whether the settlement was costless.
insights.quote: they can just like a dealer technician plug into their equipment diagnose what the failure rate is

themes.theme: 2026 as the cycle bottom and global trade disruption

insights.claim: May says the current farm-income downturn is unusual because it is global rather than the typical single-country, weather-driven shock — with simultaneous disruption across Australia, Argentina, Europe, Russia and Ukraine, plus the war in Iran affecting fertilizer and fuel flows.
insights.speaker: John May, CEO of John Deere
insights.so_what: A globally synchronized disruption removes the usual offsetting-region hedge in ag equipment demand and makes the recovery dependent on trade-policy normalization, not weather.
insights.quote: This is a global issue. We're seeing all markets right now disrupted.

insights.claim: May argues the underlying grain supply-demand balance is well matched and that the weakness is caused specifically by disrupted trade flows creating anxiety about where a crop will be sold, not by a physical glut.
insights.speaker: John May, CEO of John Deere
insights.so_what: If the problem is routing rather than balance, a trade-policy thaw could restore farm sentiment quickly — a sharper recovery than a supply-glut cycle would allow.
insights.quote: supply and demand are pretty well matched

insights.claim: Deere is intentionally underproducing retail demand to let used equipment inventory clear and stabilize the market, and believes used inventory levels are now at what would be seen at the bottom of the cycle.
insights.speaker: John May, CEO of John Deere
insights.so_what: Deliberate underproduction depresses near-term revenue but sets up an inventory-restock snapback; used-equipment inventory levels are the metric to watch for cycle timing.
insights.quote: we intentionally underproduce retail demand

insights.claim: May calls 2026 the bottom of the ag equipment cycle, citing controllable factors already fixed — normalized used inventories — plus commodity prices that are actually higher than a year ago despite the bearish narrative.
insights.speaker: John May, CEO of John Deere
insights.so_what: An explicit CEO cycle-bottom call with a stated mechanism is the setup for a 2027 order recovery; the commodity-price-up-year-over-year point contradicts common bearish framing.
insights.quote: I know you mentioned commodity prices are lower, but they're actually higher than they were a year ago

themes.theme: Connected-machine data as an open ecosystem

insights.claim: Deere's data position traces to a 2012 decision to fit machines with a telematics gateway — a cellular connection sending machine and agronomic data that was previously locked on board to a cloud platform Deere calls the Operations Center — and now spans roughly a million connected machines and 15 years of data.
insights.speaker: John May, CEO of John Deere
insights.so_what: A 15-year, million-machine agronomic dataset is the hardest asset for a competitor to replicate and the true moat behind Deere's software ambitions.
insights.quote: back in 2012, we made the decision to put a telematics gateway

insights.claim: May identifies agronomic data — seed hybrid planted, rainfall, fertilizer and pesticide timing, harvest results by field — as more valuable than machine data, because it lets growers compare multi-year decisions and query alternatives with AI tools.
insights.speaker: John May, CEO of John Deere
insights.so_what: The monetizable layer is agronomic decision support, not equipment telemetry — which is where Deere competes with agronomy and input companies rather than with machinery peers.
insights.quote: It's the aggronomic data.

insights.claim: Deere deliberately runs its data platform as an open ecosystem in which any company can connect to the data set, and the farmer chooses whether to share it with third-party agronomic providers who write prescriptions and push value back to the customer or the machine.
insights.speaker: John May, CEO of John Deere
insights.so_what: An open-platform posture reduces regulatory and right-to-repair attack surface while keeping Deere as the toll booth on prescription execution.
insights.quote: We've tried to facilitate an ecosystem where we allow any company to connect to that data set

insights.claim: When a grower consents, Deere connects crop-protection and seed input providers directly to that grower's yield, soil-type and fertility data; the provider writes a prescription that is sent straight to the planter, and Deere can then verify the exact hybrid, seed volume and spacing were applied as intended — a closed loop May says was not possible ten years ago.
insights.speaker: John May, CEO of John Deere
insights.so_what: Verified prescription execution lets input suppliers price on outcomes rather than volume, and makes Deere the mandatory execution layer between agchem and seed majors and the field.
insights.quote: That wasn't possible 10 years ago.

themes.theme: Geographic adoption, Chinese competition and weather volatility

insights.claim: May ranks precision-agriculture adoption with the US most advanced, Europe holding the same opportunity, and South America as the next market advancing at a rapid pace — while noting that very large, technologically advanced farms exist in India, Africa and Asia even where the broader country has not adopted.
insights.speaker: John May, CEO of John Deere
insights.so_what: South America is the identified next adoption wave for high-margin precision technology; emerging markets are addressed with lower-cost incremental products such as India's cell-phone-based tractor monitoring.
insights.quote: farming in America is definitely the most advanced

insights.claim: May expects Chinese equipment makers to compete first in smaller-scale agriculture such as hay production and high-value crops, and believes they remain a long way from the technology needed for large corn, soybean, cotton and sugar production systems — while Deere still sells its most advanced equipment into China's large state farms and has manufactured there since the mid-1970s.
insights.speaker: John May, CEO of John Deere
insights.so_what: Bounds the near-term Chinese competitive threat to the low end while flagging that Deere's China revenue depends on continued state-farm access — a two-sided policy exposure.
insights.quote: we're going to see them focus in more on the smaller agricultural side

insights.claim: May identifies variability and volatility in weather — not average warming — as the biggest new challenge for growers, citing parts of the US Midwest that received 20 inches of rain in a week for the first time in a decade, and corn now grown in northern US regions where it was not grown 20 years ago.
insights.speaker: John May, CEO of John Deere
insights.so_what: Rising weather variance compresses field windows further, which strengthens the autonomy value proposition and shifts crop geography — relevant to land values and seed genetics demand by region.
insights.quote: we have places in the Midwest that had 20 inches of rain in the last week. That didn't that hasn't happened in 10 years.

insights.claim: May argues that despite reduced public focus on climate, farmers invest in precision placement of nitrogen, herbicides and pesticides for stewardship reasons as well as cost, because soil and water are their production factory.
insights.speaker: John May, CEO of John Deere
insights.so_what: Suggests ag sustainability adoption is economically self-sustaining and less exposed to ESG policy reversal than sustainability spending in other sectors.
insights.quote: It is, you know, it's their factory. It's their factory where they make all their money.

insights.claim: As part of Smart Industrial, Deere removed four management layers — going from 11 layers to seven — after May observed that Blue River, the AI company Deere acquired, operated with just two layers and moved fast.
insights.speaker: John May, CEO of John Deere
insights.so_what: A concrete, auditable delayering metric — useful as a benchmark when assessing whether other legacy industrials claiming AI transformation have actually changed decision speed.
insights.quote: We had 11 layers and we went down to seven seven layers in the company.

insights.claim: May calls the move from a traditional product-line-and-region matrix to organizing around production systems — corn, soybean, wheat, cotton and sugar teams — the most successful change he has made, arguing the resulting customer depth is hard for competitors to match.
insights.speaker: John May, CEO of John Deere
insights.so_what: Crop-vertical organization, rather than machine-category organization, is the structural source of Deere's technology-attach advantage and a template competitors would have to copy wholesale.
insights.quote: you're on the corn team, you're on the soybean team, you're on the wheat team, the cotton team, the sugar team

insights.claim: Deere's hardest internal transition is shifting from a mechanical-engineering culture to software development while keeping mechanical engineers feeling valued, since scarce and hard-to-recruit software engineers cannot deliver value without the underlying hardware.
insights.speaker: John May, CEO of John Deere
insights.so_what: Software talent acquisition and retention is the practical constraint on the 2030 autonomy timeline — a bottleneck more binding than the technology itself.
insights.quote: we're going from a very mechanical engineering focused company to much more software development

insights.claim: May flags centralization-versus-decentralization as Deere's recurring open question and names centralized supply management — one team sourcing components across every industry Deere serves — as the specific function that may have gone too far and needs revisiting.
insights.speaker: John May, CEO of John Deere
insights.so_what: A CEO-flagged organizational reversal candidate; re-decentralizing sourcing would carry cost implications visible in Deere's margin commentary.
insights.quote: a supply management team that's sourcing all of our components for every industry we're in may not that may have gone too far
